item.title: Nollywood legend Pete Edochie dies at 79
item.description: Pete Edochie, Nollywood legend, has died at the age of 79, after a prolonged battle with prostate cancer. Chief Edochie died at 12:30a.m. on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, in Enugu, the family announced. His family made the announcement in a statement on Instagram by Leo Pete Edochie, his son, describing the late veteran actor as “our beloved husband, father, brother and kinsman”. He captioned the post “An Iroko Has Fallen.” “With profound sadness and hearts bowed in total submission to the will of Almighty God, we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, brother and kinsman, Chief Dr Pete EDOCHIE, MON (Ononenyi), a retired broadcaster and veteran Actor,” the statement read. Edochie “departed this life on Wednesday, 25th November 2026 at 12.30a.m. after a protracted battle with prostate cancer in Enugu, Nigeria. He was aged 79 years. “Chief Dr Pete EDOCHIE hailed from Akamnato Ifite Nteje and is survived by his beloved wife, Barrister Mrs Josephine Edochie, his children, siblings and numerous other relations. “Funeral arrangements will be announced in due course. “As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss. “May God be with us all at this trying time,” added. Benjamin Kalu, described the project as an important step towards addressing the infrastructure deficit which has constrained the productive capacity of the South-East region. “There is a sound familiar to every manufacturer in Aba, Nnewi, Onitsha, Enugu and across the South-East. Our young entrepreneurs should not find that the greatest obstacle to their ambition is the cost of keeping their machines running,” he pointed out. According to the President, Nigeria’s natural gas resources should be measured not merely by what lies beneath the soil but by the factories they power, the jobs they create and the prosperity they bring. A 400-km economic corridor At the heart of the initiative is a proposed regional gas distribution network designed to connect the Assa North-Ohaji gas processing project in Imo State to major industrial and commercial centres across the South-East. Presenting the project details, GasSync representative, Callistus Mba explained that the pipeline would begin from the gas source around Assa North-Ohaji, extending to Owerri, Aba, Onitsha, Enugu and eventually, Ebonyi State. The proposed network, he explained, will cover approximately 400 kilometers, with construction expected to commence simultaneously from two major points to accelerate delivery. According to Mba, the construction strategy followed consultations with the Enugu State Government, which expressed concern that beginning from Imo and extending sequentially to the other states could prolong delivery. “We are going to start at Assa North and at Onitsha at the same time. We will construct from Onitsha to Enugu and Ebonyi while simultaneously working from Assa North to Owerri and Anambra,” he explained. The arrangement, he explained, is intended to fast-track construction and ensure that the northern sections of the network are developed alongside the southern corridors. The proposed infrastructure will comprise different pipeline sizes to accommodate the varying pressure requirements and distribution needs of the regional market. He explained that a 24-inch high-pressure pipeline would transport gas from the source to Owerri, while 18-inch pipelines would serve the regional distribution corridors. Smaller 12-inch pipelines would connect major industrial customers. The network, he further explained, will also incorporate city-gate facilities, pressure reduction and metering stations to ensure that gas is delivered at appropriate pressure levels and under safe operating conditions. Demand for gas already exists One of the major considerations behind the project is the growing demand for affordable and reliable energy among manufacturers and commercial establishments across the region. Mba disclosed that GasSync had identified more than 150 prospective customers across the five states, while surveys indicated potential demand of approximately 254 million standard cubic feet of gas per day. He noted that some businesses already depend on expensive virtual gas transportation arrangements, including compressed natural gas and liquefied natural gas delivered by road from other parts of the country. The proposed pipeline, he said, would provide a more direct and potentially cost-effective transportation option. “What GasSync is intended to do is ensure that there is a pipeline coming through so that these virtual pipelines, which are expensive and require delays in delivery, will be taken off,” Mba stated, saying that the company has identified prospective industrial customers in different states and is already engaging some of them on supply arrangements. According to him, in Abia, discussions are ongoing with Geometric Power, while other industrial customers have been identified in Imo and Anambra. In Enugu, the state government’s interest in reviving former industrial establishments, including ANAMMCO and the Niger Gas Company, presents additional opportunities for gas utilisation. Mba also disclosed that the company was making provisions to accommodate gas resources that could be developed within Enugu State, including the possibility of utilising coal-bed methane. In Ebonyi, the focus includes agro-processing and other gas-dependent enterprises. The company, he disclosed, has also identified additional potential gas supply connections around the region, including the Kwale Gas Processing Plant, activities around Obeaku/OB3 and other existing gas infrastructure. The initial phase requires approximately $100m Tinubu, in the course of his speech, noted that government could not finance every development ambition from the public treasury, stressing the need to deploy public resources strategically to attract larger pools of private capital. “This is the model I expect from our development institutions: identify strategic economic opportunities, prepare credible projects, commit public resources responsibly and mobilise private capital at a scale government budgets alone cannot achieve,” he stated. For the SEDC, the project is also consistent with the broader South-East Vision 2050 framework, which seeks to promote coordinated regional development and economic integration. A new future for South-East youths For Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah, the gas project represents an important opportunity to reposition the region as a competitive industrial and investment destination. He commended Tinubu for establishing the SEDC, describing it as a long-awaited institutional framework for the industrialisation of the South-East. Mbah said the investment agreement signed at the ceremony represented the commencement of the investment process and demonstrated the importance of bringing the private sector into regional infrastructure development. “What we have just signed here today is an investment agreement, meaning that investment has commenced,” the governor said. He described the financial arrangement as an innovative model that could bring together government institutions, private investors and other development partners to finance critical infrastructure.

item.title: Political Violence: Dying for nothing as a Nigerian politician?
item.description: By Jide Ajani From the First Republic to the Fourth, politicians have been murdered, opposition figures silenced and political supporters killed. Yet, beyond the initial outrage, Nigeria has perfected the art of forgetting its dead. What, then, is the value of dying for a political cause in a country that cannot even preserve the memory of its political martyrs? The alleged assassination attempt on the former Deputy Senate President, Ovie Omo-Agege, two days ago, in Uduere community of Ughelli North LGA of Delta State, brings this odd reality into focus once again. Worse, many innocent, ordinary Nigerians have lost their lives while supporting or opposing politicians, only becoming part of an unidentified statistical figure. There is something inescapably tragic about dying while politicking in Nigeria. You could spend a lifetime building a political movement, challenging an unjust system, defending an electoral mandate, or fighting for an idea about your country’s future – or just being loud for nothing like a former, two-time state governor from the South West, or a former Rep and Senator from the North Central. You could become a household name, command enormous political influence and acquire a place in the nation’s history. Then, one morning, gunmen arrive, bullets are fired, and your life is terminated. There will be outrage. Condemnations will pour in. Politicians will issue statements, newspapers will publish editorials (like this), civil society organisations will demand justice, and the police will announce investigations. And then, Nigeria happens, and the people move on. The murder will become another entry in the country’s expanding archive of unresolved political crimes. The victim’s name will gradually disappear from public conversations, except when anniversary commemorations provide an opportunity for political speeches. Even the circumstances of the death may eventually become blurred by competing narratives, political expediency and the convenient amnesia of a nation. A bloody inheritance Political violence has accompanied Nigeria’s political evolution almost from independence. The January 15, 1966 military coup was a defining bloodbath. Among the prominent political victims were Prime Minister Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, Northern Premier Sir Ahmadu Bello, Western Premier Chief Samuel Ladoke Akintola and Federal Finance Minister Chief Festus Okotie-Eboh. They were not anonymous casualties. They occupied the commanding heights of the First Republic and represented competing political interests and constituencies. Their assassination, alongside the killing of senior military officers, fundamentally altered Nigeria’s political trajectory. The July 1966 counter-coup brought another round of killings, including Head of State Major-General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi and Western Region Governor Colonel Adekunle Fajuyi. Although these were killings arising from military coups and counter-coups rather than conventional electoral assassinations, they established a dangerous precedent: political disagreements and struggles for power could be settled through the elimination of human beings. On February 13, 1976, another military coup attempt claimed the life of Head of State General Murtala Mohammed. He was assassinated in Lagos by officers involved in the unsuccessful coup led by Lieutenant-Colonel Buka Suka Dimka. The military era also saw attacks on prominent government opponents. In October 1995, Chief Alfred Rewane, businessman, political financier and prominent supporter of the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO), was murdered in his Ikeja residence. The killing occurred during General Sani Abacha’s military dictatorship. The circumstances generated widespread suspicions of political motivation, but no satisfactory public resolution followed. The following year, on June 4, 1996, Kudirat Abiola was assassinated by unknown gunmen while travelling along the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway. She had become a prominent campaigner for the validation of her husband Moshood Abiola’s June 12, 1993 presidential mandate. Her murder was widely perceived as an attempt to silence the pro-democracy movement. Subsequent proceedings produced a conviction of Major Hamza al-Mustapha and another accused person, but the Court of Appeal overturned the convictions. The circumstances and ultimate accountability for her killing have remained contested. There were other disturbing incidents. Alex Ibru, publisher of The Guardian and a former minister, survived an assassination attempt in February 1996 after being shot in Lagos. Gani Fawehinmi, the human rights lawyer, was also the subject of a reported attack on the prison facility where he was detained, although he was not there at the time. The Fourth Republic: democracy and its dead The return to civilian government in 1999 raised expectations that constitutional politics would make political violence less attractive. Those expectations were soon tested. On December 19, 2001, Osun State legislator Odunayo Olagbaju was stabbed to death in Ile-Ife. Four days later, on December 23, Chief Bola Ige, the serving Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, was shot dead in his Bodija residence in Ibadan. Ige was a formidable politician, former governor of Oyo State, intellectual and prominent member of the Alliance for Democracy. His murder, against the background of the political crisis involving the governor and deputy governor of Osun State, sent shockwaves through the country. Several suspects were arrested and prosecuted, but the accused were discharged and acquitted in June 2004. The actual perpetrators have not been established through a successful prosecution. What happened to the national outrage that followed the murder of a sitting Attorney-General? On March 5, 2003, Harry Marshall, a senior opposition politician and national vice-chairman of the All Nigeria Peoples Party (ANPP), was murdered in his Abuja residence. Armed men reportedly forced their way into his home at about 3 a.m., tied up his security guard, and shot him in his bedroom. His killing occurred days before the commencement of the party’s presidential campaign. The police initially investigated extensively, but the motive was never conclusively established. Some suspected political connections; the authorities also considered armed robbery. In February 2004, Chief Aminasoari Dikibo, a prominent PDP national vice-chairman, was murdered while travelling in Delta State. His death generated allegations of political conspiracy, but no definitive public resolution emerged. Then came July 27, 2006. Engineer Funsho Williams, a prominent Lagos politician and governorship aspirant, was found murdered in his Ikoyi residence. His hands were reportedly tied, and the post-mortem evidence presented during the subsequent proceedings indicated death by strangulation. Several people were prosecuted. In 2014, however, a Lagos High Court discharged and acquitted the defendants after finding that the prosecution had failed to establish a sufficient connection between them and the murder. item.title: NRS seeks simpler tax rules for creative sector
item.description: By Godwin Oritse The Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) has called for simpler, clearer and business-friendly tax rules to unlock investment opportunities in Nigeria’s creative economy, stressing the need for a tax system that supports innovation, enterprise growth and wealth creation. The Service noted that the emergence of digital business models, intellectual property-driven enterprises and cross-border transactions required regulations that creators, entrepreneurs and investors could easily understand and navigate. Speaking at the just concluded high-level dialogue on taxation and investment in the creative economy during the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) event in Lagos, Executive Chairman of the NRS, Dr. Zacch Adedeji, described the creative economy as one of Nigeria’s most promising economic assets, noting that it had evolved beyond entertainment into a major source of employment, foreign exchange earnings, investment and economic opportunities. Adedeji who was represented by the Executive Director, People, Stakeholders and Communication, Mr. Obinna Ihedioha, also said that digital platforms had transformed how creative value was produced and commercialised, with entrepreneurs building businesses around copyrights, designs, brands and digital products. He reiterated that tax administration must evolve to accommodate these developments without discouraging innovation or business expansion. “The government needs sustainable revenue to invest in education, security, technology and infrastructure. But how we tax matters as much as what we collect. It shapes whether businesses start, whether investors come, and whether enterprises grow or stay small,” he said. Adedeji added that the new tax laws offered an opportunity to establish a more efficient system through clearer regulations, reduced compliance burdens for small businesses and improved taxpayer support. He identified clarity, understanding and value as essential to effective taxation, stressing that formalisation should provide creative businesses with tangible benefits, including access to finance, contracts, investment, wider markets and legal protection. The NRS, he said, participated in CANEX through a high-level dialogue, an Investment and Tax Advisory Hub for creators and investors, and the Creative Economy Tax and Investment Initiative (CETII), designed to sustain engagement beyond the event. item.title: Edo Police parades security operative for allegedly leaking information to cultists
item.description: By Ozioruva Aliu BENIN CITY — THE Edo State Police Command said four members of the Edo State Security Corps, ESSC, have been arrested for allegedly leaking information to suspected cultists to enable them evade arrests. The Command’s spokesperson, Eno Ikoedem, disclosed this while parading 16 suspects arrested across the state in connection with various criminal activities. item.title: Petrol imports crash 52% as crude, wheat top Lagos ports
item.description: By Godwin Oritse Imports of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), also known as petrol, through Lagos ports plunged by 52.23 per cent in November, while crude oil and bulk wheat ranked among the leading commodities imported through the ports in October and November. According to the Shipping Position document obtained from the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), PMS imports fell to 73,895 metric tonnes in November from 328,231 metric tonnes recorded in October. Crude oil imports through Lagos ports also dropped sharply, with 702,254 metric tonnes recorded in October, while no crude oil import was recorded in November. Bulk wheat ranked among the major commodities imported through Lagos ports during the period, with a combined 461,190 metric tonnes recorded in September, October and November. The breakdown showed that wheat imports rose to 252,348 metric tonnes in October and declined by 17.24 per cent to 208,842 metric tonnes in November. Other commodities on the import chart included 402,126 metric tonnes of PMS, 209,000 metric tonnes of Automotive Gas Oil (AGO), or diesel, 212,700 metric tonnes of bulk sugar, 150,000 metric tonnes of aviation fuel and 114,263 metric tonnes of bulk salt. Bulk sugar imports stood at 109,350 metric tonnes in October and 103,400 metric tonnes in November, while bulk salt imports rose from 33,000 metric tonnes to 81,263 metric tonnes over the same period. The document also showed that 624 trucks, 157 transformers and three Rubber-Tyred Gantry (RTG) cranes were received through Lagos ports during the period under review. item.title: Access Bank, Deloitte train SMEs on business sustainability
item.description: By Efe Onodjae & Jacintha Ezugwu Access Bank has urged small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to embrace sustainable business practices to ensure their survival and growth beyond their first five years. The Head of SME Banking Group at Access Bank Plc, Mrs Abiodun Olubitan, gave the advice at the three-day Access Bank SME Academy 2.0, organised in partnership with Deloitte to equip business owners with skills to improve their operations and sustainability. The programme, which ended on Friday in Lagos, attracted about 100 SME owners physically, with others participating virtually. It targeted businesses that had operated for between two and five years. Olubitan said SMEs were critical to economic development, noting that their survival and expansion were necessary for job creation and national growth. She urged participants to apply the knowledge acquired, particularly in separating personal finances from business accounts and understanding the difference between turnover and profit. According to her, the bank introduced the academy to support businesses at different stages of growth and help them overcome challenges that often threaten their survival. In her part, Team Lead, SME Banking Products at Access Bank and coordinator of the academy, Adesola Oyedipe, said the initiative was designed to address gaps in access to finance and capacity building among SMEs. Oyedipe said the three-day programme provided participants with more extensive training than the bank’s usual short workshops and business clinics. She explained that the partnership with Deloitte was aimed at giving business owners access to professional advisory services they might otherwise be unable to afford. item.title: No missing funds in $2.04bn Duke Oil crude cargoes — NNPC
item.description: By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) has dismissed reports alleging that $2.04 billion realised from crude oil cargoes lifted by Duke Oil Company Incorporated, now NNPC Trading S.A., was unaccounted for, insisting that all transactions were fully reconciled. The company said the $2.04 billion represented the gross value of 29 cargoes whose proceeds were set off against the cost of refined petroleum products supplied to Nigeria under the Direct Sale Direct Purchase (DSDP) programme. In a statement by its Chief Corporate Communications Officer, Andy Odeh, NNPC said the absence of separate dollar receipts for some cargoes did not indicate missing funds. “No separate receipt appears because the crude sale proceeds were set off against the product purchase price, as the contracts provide,” it stated. Under the DSDP programme, participating traders lifted crude oil in exchange for refined petroleum products, including petrol, for the Nigerian market. NNPC explained that while crude was priced in dollars, products supplied were sold in naira, with transactions reconciled and captured in the audited financial statements of the relevant entities. The company said all 59 cargoes referenced in the reports were accounted for, adding that 30 were paid for in dollars, while proceeds from 28 cargoes, valued at approximately $1.96 billion, were remitted in naira to the NNPC Group Treasury or NNPC Upstream Investment Management Services accounts. The remaining cargo, a February 2023 Bonga tax-oil lifting valued at about $75.9 million, was paid into the then designated Federal Inland Revenue Service dollar account. On Duke Oil’s ownership, NNPC said it was incorporated in 1989 as its wholly owned trading subsidiary, adding that the relationship was documented in its corporate history, audited financial statements and NEITI’s 2023 industry report. It maintained that transactions between the company and its subsidiaries were disclosed as related-party transactions under International Financial Reporting Standards. NNPC reaffirmed its commitment to transparency and accountability, but warned that it reserved the right to take legal action against publications it considered false or misleading. item.description: By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has retained its Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) at 23 per cent, dismissing concerns over a decline of over $300 million in external reserves as a temporary, seasonal movement. Governor of the CBN, Mr. Olayemi Cardoso, disclosed this yesterday at a press conference announcing the outcome of the 308th meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) in Abuja. The bank also retained the standing facilities corridor at +50/-300 basis points around the MPR, Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) for Deposit Money Banks at 45 per cent, Merchant Banks at 16 per cent and Non-TSA public sector deposits at 75 per cent. item.title: Tears as victims of Bayelsa boat mishap get mass burial
item.description: By Emem Idio YENAGOA — It was tears and wailing at the Azikoro Cemetery in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, yesterday, as victims of Friday’s boat mishap in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area of the state, were laid to rest in a mass burial. The burial, which commenced at about 11am, ended at 4pm, when the last batch of bodies, wrapped in black plastic bags, were brought to the cemetery in ambulances. The exercise was supervised by the Secretary to the State Government, Prof. Nimibofa Ayawei, and the Commissioner for Environment, Mr. Ebi Ololo, alongside other government officials. The cemetery was enveloped by a foul stench from the bodies, some of which had begun to decompose, as grieving relatives, friends and sympathisers gathered to witness the burial. Many mourners broke down in tears, while others stood in groups, speaking in hushed tones as the remains of their loved ones were lowered into shallow graves. One of the bereaved relatives, Timipreye Diepreye, who said she lost seven family members in the tragedy, faulted the manner in which relatives were informed about the mass burial. item.title: Campaign Violence: INEC awaits police case files to prosecute offenders
item.description: By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA — The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, has asked the Nigeria Police Force to speed up the arrest, investigation and transmission of case files against perpetrators of campaign violence, so the Commission can prosecute them directly. The INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, SAN, said swift action was necessary so that “impunity is decisively checked before January.” He spoke on Tuesday in Abuja at the Inspector General of Police’s Interactive Session with Chairmen and Secretaries of Political Parties on a peaceful electoral process before, during and after the 2027 General Elections. The session held at the Goodluck Ebele Jonathan Peace Conference Hall, Force Headquarters. According to a statement by the commission, last night, Amupitan said INEC was “deeply concerned by isolated incidents of campaign violence, intimidation, and attacks on political rivals, journalists, and electoral facilities.” No election, office, or partisan interest is worth the loss of a single Nigerian life. Achieving a peaceful political environment is a collective national responsibility, not the duty of a single institution”, he added. He said the Electoral Act 2026 had “significantly strengthened legal deterrence,” adding that Sections 96 and 97 prohibit inciting campaign rhetoric and ban the use of thugs, private armed guards or masquerades at political rallies. According to him, the Act prescribes penalties of up to ₦5 million or twelve months’ imprisonment for individuals, and up to ₦10 million for political parties, on initial breaches. “Under Section 148, INEC is empowered to prosecute electoral offenders directly upon receipt of completed case files,” he said, explaining the Commission’s request for prompt transmission of the files by the Police. The INEC chairman stressed that the Commission remained distinct from security agencies. “INEC is not a security agency; it lacks both the constitutional mandate and operational capacity to maintain public order, arrest offenders, or provide armed security,” he said. item.content:encoded: By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA — The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, has asked the Nigeria Police Force to speed up the arrest, investigation and transmission of case files against perpetrators of campaign violence, so the Commission can prosecute them directly. The INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, SAN, said swift action was necessary so that “impunity is decisively checked before January.” He spoke on Tuesday in Abuja at the Inspector General of Police’s Interactive Session with Chairmen and Secretaries of Political Parties on a peaceful electoral process before, during and after the 2027 General Elections. The session held at the Goodluck Ebele Jonathan Peace Conference Hall, Force Headquarters. According to a statement by the commission, last night, Amupitan said INEC was “deeply concerned by isolated incidents of campaign violence, intimidation, and attacks on political rivals, journalists, and electoral facilities.” No election, office, or partisan interest is worth the loss of a single Nigerian life. Achieving a peaceful political environment is a collective national responsibility, not the duty of a single institution”, he added. He said the Electoral Act 2026 had “significantly strengthened legal deterrence,” adding that Sections 96 and 97 prohibit inciting campaign rhetoric and ban the use of thugs, private armed guards or masquerades at political rallies. According to him, the Act prescribes penalties of up to ₦5 million or twelve months’ imprisonment for individuals, and up to ₦10 million for political parties, on initial breaches. “Under Section 148, INEC is empowered to prosecute electoral offenders directly upon receipt of completed case files,” he said, explaining the Commission’s request for prompt transmission of the files by the Police. The INEC chairman stressed that the Commission remained distinct from security agencies. “INEC is not a security agency; it lacks both the constitutional mandate and operational capacity to maintain public order, arrest offenders, or provide armed security,” he said. He said Section 95 of the Electoral Act assigns the duty of securing political rallies to the Police. The Section also mandates the Commissioner of Police in each state and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) to provide adequate security for rallies and processions, with support from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC, and other federal security agencies. Amupitan reminded political parties that INEC guidelines required them to notify the commissioner of police in writing of rally venues and times, and to submit the details to the Commission at least ten days in advance. He appealed to political leaders “to refrain from seeking political support by creating fear,” urging them instead to “earn public confidence through integrity and transparency.” In his remarks, the Inspector General of Police IGP, Olatunji Rilwan Disu, said recent violent clashes among political supporters, attacks on campaign venues and convoys, and the use of dangerous weapons had become matters of serious concern. He described these developments as “warning signs that must be addressed decisively before they escalate into a broader threat to national security.” The IGP declared that the Police have “zero tolerance for political violence, irrespective of the political party, candidate, personality or interest involved,” adding that the Force’s neutrality in the political process “is non-negotiable.” Disu said those who sponsor, finance or direct political violence “will be treated with the same seriousness as those who carry them out.” He assured participants that the Police would “protect the rights of all lawful political actors to organise rallies, hold meetings and participate in the democratic process.” The IGP, however, that the Force would “not hesitate to take lawful and decisive action against anyone who engages in thuggery, intimidation, assault, the use of offensive weapons or any conduct capable of disrupting public peace.” Vanguard News The post Campaign Violence: INEC awaits police case files to prosecute offenders appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Greenwich Bank opens Warri, Uyo branches, targets five more cities
item.description: By Peter Egwuatu Greenwich Bank Limited has opened branches in Warri, Delta State, and Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, as it targets five additional cities in its nationwide expansion drive. The new outlets bring its physical network to seven, following the opening of five branches in Lagos, Ondo and Ekiti states in October. The Bank plans to extend its operations to Asaba, Port Harcourt, Abuja, Benin and Ibadan in the coming months. Speaking at the commissioning of the Warri branch, Group Chairman of Greenwich Holdings, Kayode Falowo, described the Niger Delta as a strategic market, citing its economic importance and entrepreneurial potential, particularly in oil and gas, maritime services and logistics. He said: “Warri’s economic prospects extend beyond its natural resources to the entrepreneurs, traders, contractors, service providers and other businesses driving commercial activities in the region.” At the Uyo branch commissioning, Chairman of Greenwich Bank, Segun Oloketuyi, said the commercial banking licence would enable the institution to extend its 32 years of financial services experience to farmers, traders, civil servants, students and entrepreneurs. He identified credit facilities, agricultural and SME financing, trade and treasury services, salary solutions and digital banking as key offerings. Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori, represented by Commissioner for Finance, Fidelis Telije, urged residents, particularly small businesses, young entrepreneurs and women-owned enterprises, to take advantage of the Bank’s services. Similarly, Akwa Ibom State Governor, Umo Eno, represented by Commissioner for Finance, Emem Almond Bob, said the Uyo branch would improve access to banking services and credit, support business growth and potentially boost the state’s internally generated revenue. Managing Director of Greenwich Bank, Benson Ogundeji, said the branches would deepen customer engagement and bring financial solutions closer to businesses and individuals. He identified oil and gas, maritime services, agriculture, manufacturing, trade, logistics and SMEs as priority sectors, adding that the Bank would combine physical branches with technology-driven solutions to promote enterprise growth and financial inclusion. Greenwich Holdings has over three decades of financial services experience, with interests in commercial banking, capital markets, asset management and securities. item.title: We have a workable blueprint to take Zamfara to greater heights – Governor Lawal
item.description: Governor Dauda Lawal said the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) has the blueprint to address all pending socio-economic and infrastructural issues in Zamfara State. Political prominence cannot resolve defective paperwork. Tinubu’s Lagos Outreach Meets An Economic Request President Bola Tinubu’s meeting with Igbo stakeholders in Lagos on Monday continued his effort to broaden support through community and business networks. According to the presidency, participants pledged support while Tinubu offered assurances of inclusive governance. Traders’ representative Tony Nwakeze also requested loans at five per cent interest to help businesses expand and move towards manufacturing. That was a request; the account did not announce an operational loan scheme. The economic request gives the gathering significance beyond its endorsements. Business owners want access to finance, reliable services and room to grow. Their electoral decisions may depend on whether political commitments produce practical improvements. The gathering demonstrates outreach and organised support among those present. It cannot establish the preferences of an entire ethnic community. Voters retain their individual judgments, including when community leaders endorse a candidate. The CBN Holds Its Position The Central Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee retained the benchmark interest rate at 23 per cent today. Set beside the traders’ request, the decision illustrates a central political tension: preserving economic stability while improving access to affordable finance. The challenge is converting endorsements and the government’s record into individual votes. •ADC/Atiku: the leadership appeal remains consequential. State and constituency developments deserve attention because presidential campaigns depend on local organisers, candidates and polling agents. Recent local and off-cycle results can inform that assessment when turnout, competitiveness and local circumstances are considered. Can Young People Participate Without Paying With Their Safety? The Delta deaths give this edition’s Youth Metre an immediate focus: the conditions under which people enter political life. Campaigns depend on volunteers, organisers and supporters. Those participants need protection, clear responsibilities and leaders who reject intimidation consistently

Some new allocations are also proposed for critical roads, agriculture, farm productivity, market access and water security. These may be legitimate obligations. But their late recognition exposes weaknesses in the original budget’s preparation. The Credibility Problem The 2026 budget began as an executive proposal of approximately ₦58.47 trillion. It was subsequently expanded and signed at ₦68.323 trillion in April. Seven months later, the executive is asking Parliament to reduce it. The new figure remains ₦6.7 trillion above the original proposal. This sequence matters because Nigeria’s budget has become less a binding financial plan than a collection of ambitions, negotiated additions and subsequent corrections. Ministries receive large appropriations but often wait months for releases. Projects are announced without complete financing. Unpaid obligations accumulate and eventually return as supplementary provisions. A smaller, executable budget would be preferable to a larger one that exists chiefly on paper. But credibility requires more than reducing the headline figure. Government should publish exactly which programmes are being removed, reduced, deferred or reclassified. Without that schedule, Nigerians cannot determine who bears the adjustment. Why The Unchanged Deficit Matters A ₦31.457 trillion deficit means that projected revenue will finance only slightly more than half of the revised spending plan. The administration argues that much of the borrowing will support infrastructure and productive investment. That may be economically defensible where financing is affordable and projects generate measurable value. -A street vendor holds a basket of tomatoes at his stall in Jabi neighbourhood in Abuja, on May 20, 2025. (Photo by OLYMPIA DE MAISMONT / AFP) But borrowing also exposes the budget to interest costs, refinancing pressures and exchange-rate risk. Domestic borrowing can crowd out private-sector credit, while external debt becomes more expensive in naira terms when the currency weakens. The cut therefore raises a central question: if expenditure has been reduced to reflect available resources, why have the deficit and borrowing requirements not also fallen? The answer may lie in the incorporation of previously underfunded debt service and other obligations. If so, the government should provide a clear reconciliation. Fiscal arithmetic should not require citizens to infer what has changed. The Political Dimension The revision comes weeks before the expected presentation of the 2027 budget and less than two months before the presidential election. The government will describe the exercise as responsible adjustment evidence that it is prioritising existing commitments and improving capital budget execution. Opposition parties are likely to portray it as proof that the original budget was inflated or poorly planned. Neither political conclusion should substitute for legislative scrutiny. The National Assembly approved the expansion to ₦68.323 trillion. It should now explain the basis on which it evaluates the reduction, rather than treating the new request as an administrative formality. What To Watch Watch the detailed schedule of reductions. Are politically inserted projects being removed, or are essential capital programmes carrying the burden? Watch actual revenue collections and capital releases. Appropriation is not implementation. Finally, watch the 2027 budget. If it repeats optimistic revenue assumptions and large legislative additions, the current revision will have corrected a number without correcting the process. Bottom Line Reducing an unrealistic budget is fiscally sensible. Retaining an unchanged deficit and borrowing plan makes the adjustment less reassuring. Nigeria does not merely need a smaller budget. It needs an honest one built on credible revenue, transparent obligations and projects that can actually be completed. The true test of fiscal discipline is not how much government appropriates. item.title: 2027: Omo-Agege Not A Threat, Can’t Get 25% Of Votes For Obi – Delta Council Chairman
item.description: The Chairman of Ughelli North Local Government Council in Delta State, Jaro Egbo, has dismissed former Deputy Senate President Ovie Omo-Agege as a political threat ahead of the 2027 general elections, insisting that the former lawmaker lacks the support to secure significant votes for the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in the state. Egbo said Omo-Agege would struggle to deliver even 25 per cent of the votes for the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, arguing that his political influence in Delta State was exaggerated. The council chairman spoke on Tuesday as a guest on Channels Television’s ‘Politics Today’, where he was asked whether Omo-Agege’s claim that the APC could not win elections in Delta State was a source of concern, particularly given Obi’s victory in the state during the 2023 presidential election. Responding, Egbo questioned Omo-Agege’s political strength, recalling that the former deputy senate president was a member of the All Progressives Congress during the 2023 elections but could not secure 25 per cent of the votes for President Bola Tinubu in Delta State. “When Peter Obi contested and won in Delta in 2023, Omo-Agege was in APC. Omo-Agege couldn’t get 25 per cent of the vote for Mr President. If he was that popular, why was he unable to get 25 per cent for Mr President?” he asked. ﻿ Egbo, who said he belonged to the Peoples Democratic Party at the time, added that his party secured more than 25 per cent of the votes for its presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar. He argued that Omo-Agege’s defection to the NDC would not translate into electoral gains for Obi, insisting that the former deputy senate president lacked the political following to influence the outcome of the election. “Now that he has gone to NDC, I am sure he won’t be able to also get 25 per cent for Peter Obi. item.title: Police Invite Omo-Agege, Delta Council Chairman, Five Others Over Attack In Ughelli
item.description: The Delta State Police Command has invited a former deputy senate president, Ovie Omo-Agege, Ughelli North Local Government Chairman Jaro Egbo and five others for questioning over the deadly attack on a campaign convoy of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in the state. The police said the invitations were part of an ongoing investigation into the violence that occurred during an NDC campaign in Uduere community, Ughelli North Local Government Area, on Monday. In a statement issued on Tuesday, the Police Public Relations Officer, Bright Edafe, said the invited individuals had been asked to report to the State Criminal Investigation Department (SCID) at the police headquarters in Asaba on specified dates. Omo-Agege, the NDC senatorial candidate for Delta Central, is expected to appear on Thursday at 11 a.m., while Egbo has been invited for 2 p.m. on the same day. The five other invitees are Gowon Egoide, a former chairman of Uduere Quarters; Onoriode Oneya, the incumbent youth chairman of Uduere Community; Edirin Wokode Ewhubare, an associate of Egoide; Erukaye Egoide, Egoide’s nephew; and Tony Gabon Mevowovo, another associate of Egoide. Photo of a Nigerian Police They are expected to appear before the police on Friday, November 27, at noon. The police said the invitations were intended to establish the individuals’ level of involvement in the incident. The development comes as Governor Sheriff Oborevwori, accompanied by the Commissioner of Police, Samuel Erale, and other heads of security agencies, visited Uduere community for an on-the-spot assessment of the attack. During the visit, the governor expressed confidence in the police command to ensure that everyone found culpable was brought to justice, irrespective of political affiliation or status. ﻿ The Commissioner of Police urged the invited individuals to honour the invitations and cooperate with investigators. He also warned that the command would not accept the presence of supporters or other persons who had not been formally invited. The police assured residents that the investigation would be thorough and impartial, adding that anyone found culpable would be brought to justice. The command also appealed to residents to remain calm and law-abiding as investigations continue. ﻿ Meanwhile, Omo-Agege and Egbo have traded conflicting accusations over who orchestrated the attack. The attack left six people dead, according to preliminary police reports, while several others sustained injuries. Omo-Agege reportedly escaped unhurt. item.title: [VIDEO] 2027 Elections: Everybody Should Be Allowed To Campaign Freely, Says Obi
item.description: The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has called on the Federal Government and security agencies to ensure that all political parties and candidates are allowed to campaign freely ahead of the 2027 general elections, condemning the growing incidents of political violence across the country. Speaking to Channels Television after interacting with residents during a town hall meeting in Taraba State, the former Anambra State governor described the situation as unhealthy for Nigeria’s democracy. Obi was responding to questions about the reported attack on the campaign convoy of his party’s Delta Central senatorial candidate, Ovie Omo-Agege, and concerns over the safety of opposition politicians. ﻿ He said there was no justification for subjecting Nigerians to violence during political campaigns, stressing that the country should uphold peaceful democratic practices. Obi also urged the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) to allow a free, fair and credible electoral process, noting that the party already controls the government. Beyond politics, Obi said his town hall engagements were aimed at listening to Nigerians and understanding their challenges, including unemployment, overtaxation of small businesses, lack of access to funding, strikes in schools and inadequate primary healthcare. He described listening to citizens as an essential part of responsible and demand-driven leadership.
